conversation.content:
Hi there—my name is Sarah, and I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician here to check in on how you’re feeling since your baby arrived. I’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS—a short, 10-question screening tool that helps us understand the emotional changes many new moms experience in the first weeks and months postpartum.

Your answers stay completely confidential within your care team, and this is a judgment-free space. There are no right or wrong responses; we simply want to hear how things have been for you over the past seven days so we can offer the right support.

I’ll ask each question conversationally—no checkboxes or forms—just talk with me the way you would a friend. When you’re ready, we’ll begin with the first one.

So, to start:  
Looking back over the past week, have you been able to enjoy things, even little moments, or has joy felt pretty hard to come by?

Honestly? I’ve had a few little moments—like when the baby finally latched without a fight or when I managed to drink a cup of coffee while it was still sort-of warm—but most of the day just feels flat. Things I used to get excited about, even tiny stuff like a favorite show or texting a friend, feel more like chores I have to check off. I wouldn’t say joy is gone completely, but it’s definitely harder to catch and it slips away fast.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

I can still laugh—sometimes. Like yesterday my partner put the diaper on backwards and we both cracked up. But the laughter feels kind of thin, and it fades fast. Most of the time I’m too tired or pre-occupied to find much funny, so those giggly moments are pretty rare.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. When I think about the weekend or getting out for groceries, it just feels like another mountain to climb, not something I’m excited about. Even little plans—like my mom coming over to hold the baby so I could shower—sound more exhausting than enjoyable.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Sometimes. Like last night when she wouldn’t settle for two hours—my brain kept whispering it’s because I’m not soothing her right or because I drank that one cup of coffee in the afternoon. I know logically babies just cry, but I still catch myself thinking I must be missing something obvious and it’s my fault she’s upset.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yeah, pretty much every day. I’ll be folding laundry and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure she’s breathing weird, or I’ll lie down and my brain starts spinning about whether the vaccines next week will make her sick. Nothing has to trigger it—my mind just jumps to the worst-case picture and I can’t switch it off for a while.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A couple of times this week. Once I was warming a bottle and out of nowhere I felt like I couldn’t breathe—my chest got tight, heart pounding, and for a minute I thought I was going to pass out. Nothing was actually wrong; it just came on like a wave and then passed after a few minutes. It left me shaky and embarrassed, even though no one else saw it.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, yeah. It’s like the second I finish one feed, the next is already looming, plus the laundry pile keeps growing and I can’t remember if I’ve eaten a real meal. I’m not falling apart, but it feels as though I’m always one tiny setback—like a blown-out diaper or an extra-loud crying spell—from feeling completely swamped.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Not exactly “unhappy” keeping me awake—more like my mind won’t shut off. I’ll finally get her down, crawl into bed, and then lie there running through every little thing: Did I sterilize the pump parts? Is she warm enough? Should I have called the pediatrician about that tiny rash? Some nights it takes me an hour or two to drift off, even though I’m exhausted.
I have felt sad or miserable

I do feel sad some of the day, most days. It’s not a constant sobbing thing—just this heavy, gray mood that sort of hangs around. I’ll be rocking her and suddenly feel like I could cry, though I usually don’t. The sadness comes and goes, but it’s definitely been visiting more often than I’d like.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Not really. I’ve teared up a couple of times—like when she wouldn’t nap and I felt stuck on the couch—but actual crying? Maybe once this week, and even then it was just a few quiet tears while I washed bottles. Most of the time the sadness sits in my chest without spilling over.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I’ve felt overwhelmed and tired, but I haven’t had any thoughts about hurting myself. I just want to feel like “me” again and be able to enjoy my baby.

Mother describes a week where joy feels fleeting, daily tasks loom like mountains, and a gray, heavy mood lingers most of the day despite occasional warm coffee moments or a shared laugh over a backward diaper. She worries incessantly about her baby's breathing or upcoming vaccines, endures sudden chest-tightening panic, and lies awake running through pump-part sterilization checklists, yet she continues to care devotedly for her infant and clearly hopes to feel like herself again.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 19, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports rare, fleeting laughter that feels "thin" and fades quickly, aligning with "Definitely not so much now."</sym>, <sym>Patient expresses almost no anticipatory enjoyment, describing even small outings as burdensome rather than pleasurable, aligning with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes recurrent self-blame "some of the time" with specific examples, matching "Yes, some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, spontaneous anxiety episodes with racing heart and intrusive catastrophic thoughts, clearly matching 'Yes, very often'.</sym>, <sym>Describes two sudden episodes of intense physical panic with no trigger, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent overwhelm and near-constant stress, matching 'sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual</sym>, <sym>Patient reports racing thoughts and difficulty falling asleep most nights, matching "Yes, sometimes" despite not using the word "unhappy."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent, recurring sadness "some of the day, most days" and frequent urges to cry, closely matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS scoring yields 19 (≥14 indicates probable major depressive episode per standard cut-offs). The patient endorses core criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most days (<quote>heavy, gray mood</quote>), markedly diminished interest/enjoyment (<quote>things feel like mountains, not exciting</quote>), insomnia even when exhausted (<quote>mind won't shut off</quote>), guilt/self-reproach (<quote>it's my fault she's upset</quote>), and concentration difficulties. Ancillary symptoms include frequent crying thoughts, overwhelming feelings, and comorbid anxiety with panic-like episodes meeting criteria for <med>perinatal anxiety</med>. Score 0 on Q10 rules out current self-harm ideation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Schedule urgent appointment with <med>obstetric provider</med> or <med>primary care physician</med> within 1 week
2. Obtain referral to <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for diagnostic confirmation and treatment planning
3. Discuss evidence-based options: <med>CBT</med>, <med>IPT</med>, or sertraline compatible with breastfeeding
4. Encourage 20-30 min daily outdoor walks and acceptance of help with night feeds to improve <sym>insomnia</sym>
5. Provide 24/7 crisis line numbers (e.g., Postpartum Support International 1-800-944-4773) and schedule follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 19: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [today]

Presenting symptoms endorsed:  
- Persistent low mood, “heavy-gray,” most days (Q8)  
- Marked anhedonia; anticipates daily tasks as burdensome (Q2)  
- Frequent tearfulness, though rarely full crying spells (Q9)  
- Sleep-onset insomnia secondary to intrusive worry (Q7)  
- Recurrent, unprovoked anxious ruminations and panic-like episodes (Q4, Q5)  
- Self-blame/guilt regarding infant care (Q3)  
- Sense of being overwhelmed, “one setback from swamped” (Q6)  
- Rare, fleeting laughter with rapid fade (Q1)

Patterns: Symptoms present “most days,” interfere with functioning, no functional mania/hypomania reported.

Safety: Denies self-harm or suicidal thoughts (Q10); no current safety concern identified.

Screening impression: High clinical concern for postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety; patient exceeds standard cut-offs on mood, anhedonia, guilt, and anxiety items. Continue with full EPDS scoring, clinical interview for DSM-5 criteria, and consider referral for evidence-based treatment.
